cells.tense: You are the one carrying what you imagined, and you are still holding it up.
cells.ask: Say what you want one time, out loud, and then let them answer.
cells.core:
You can say what you want without dressing it up first, and you don't need anyone to approve it before you mean it. What you imagined is real enough to you — you feel it, and it holds, and that's most of why it works. You count things and you don't stop counting. Somewhere in a room someone is deciding something that's yours to decide.

You've already answered for something this week and brought it back into the open. That's the shape of it: you ask, they answer, and nothing has to be undone afterward. Today it can tip the other way — you read the room before you speak, and by the time you've decided what's fair it's already happening. Ask for one thing plainly, once, and then let it sit where they put it.

cells.tense: You will be bracing for the moment this comes apart before anyone has even moved.
cells.ask: Choose one thing that's growing badly and let it be, for now.
cells.core:
You're ahead of it — you've already seen who ends up owing what and how this gets unfair, and you're trying to settle it before it opens. You're treating what's not balanced yet as if it already broke. Closing that gap early keeps things square, but it costs you the part where it gets to work itself out.

Loosened up, watching something grow doesn't mean holding it — you handle what needs handling and leave the rest where it is until it moves. You're carrying what hasn't happened. Pick one thing you're managing ahead of schedule, and this week leave it alone where it sits. Nothing gets worse from one week of not arranging it.

cells.tense: You kept walking past the moment when what you wanted could have been said out loud.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you want. Then say it to one person.
cells.core:
You know what you want, and somewhere along the line you stopped saying it. So now the room runs on what other people bring, and you keep the wider picture to yourself. None of that left. What left was the moment where you could put something on the table and let it count.

When this is working, it's simple: you name what you want before you're sure it's fair, and you let the answer land where it lands. That's still yours to do. Nothing in you is broken from having waited; you just haven't used it in a while. Write one thing down for yourself, then say it to one person this week, accepting whatever they do with it.

cells.tense: You are already making fair calls, and you talk about it as if the room were doing the deciding.
cells.ask: Pick one call you make and say it was yours.
cells.core:
You're already keeping things level — saying what's useful, adjusting when something tips, staying with what's actually here. It works, and it works well enough that you don't call it a keeping. You call it reading what's in the room, which is what it looks like from the inside.

Somebody's going to bring up fairness soon, and you'll want to get it right. Before that conversation, take one call you made this week — one small call — and write it down as yours. Not as what the situation required. As something you decided. Then you'll know which decisions these are, and the next one will be easier to say out loud.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is satisfied with what they actually imagined and felt — the record says self-praise may be at stake, so I avoid making the record's description of the card sound like a verdict on their state; the reader could reasonably say 'I'm not satisfied at all, I'm just not fighting what's here.' The asks are still useful if I'm wrong about which of those is happening, because each is an action that works regardless of whether the diagnosis is about satisfaction or exhaustion. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that would make them feel praised for not counting — the plain thing is the asking-and-answering, not the not-tallying.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's balance here is about speaking up or staying silent on what they want; Equity can be running on any exchange, and I may be reading my own first draft's theme back in. The reader could reasonably say the leveling is in how they split work, money, or time — not in whether they say what they want. Each ask survives that: asking for one thing plainly, leaving one managed thing alone, writing down one want, or claiming one call all work whether the imbalance is spoken or unspoken. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the one that makes waiting or not-counting sound noble; the plain thing is the asking and the answering, not the not-tallying.
